title: Why AI is making us adapt to technology instead of the reverse
excerpt: AI isn't just changing the world around us, innovation theorist John Nosta says. It's changing how humans adapt, think, and solve problems.
content_html:
'The Great Inversion': Why one innovation theorist says technology is no longer adapting to us — we're adapting to it

By Thibault Spirlet

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Humans have long built technologies to change the world around them — faster cars, better tools, and more efficient machines.

AI may be among the first widely adopted technologies that not only shapes the world around us but also increasingly influences how we think, learn, and solve problems.

That's according to John Nosta, an innovation theorist and founder of the think tank NostaLab, who called the shift "The Great Inversion."

"Progress seems to be increasingly about making humans better for the technological world we've created," Nosta told Business Insider.

'The organism is the project'

Historically, many innovations have helped people overcome physical constraints, he said. Humans invented the wheel to make it easier to move heavy loads, and the car dramatically expanded how far and fast people could travel, for example.

Nosta says that AI is different because its primary impact is often cognitive rather than physical. Instead of simply changing people's environment, he says, AI increasingly changes how they approach thinking, reasoning, and decision-making.

"We're now into the cognitive age, where what's changing is the nature of thought," he said. "The path from A to B is getting shorter and shorter, and we are deferring cognition to the machine."

His view echoes a growing body of research suggesting that AI can influence how people learn, remember information, and make decisions.

Researchers at Oxford University Press warned last year that generative AI can make students faster and more fluent while quietly reducing the depth of learning that comes from pausing, questioning, and working through problems independently.

Meanwhile, a report from the Work AI Institute found that AI often creates an illusion of expertise, making users feel more capable even as some underlying skills begin to erode.

For Nosta, AI is one example of a broader trend. He points to GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, which were originally developed to treat diabetes but are now widely used for weight loss and are being studied for their potential to reduce cravings for alcohol, nicotine, and compulsive behaviors.

Rather than redesigning environments to better suit people, some new innovations modify human behavior to help people function within existing environments, he said. "The organism is the project."

That shift, he said, carries important implications for human cognition.

Using AI as a partner, not a replacement

Still, Nosta doesn't believe AI is inherently harmful.

He distinguishes between what he calls "iterative intelligence," where people use AI to deepen their understanding through conversation, and "cognitive surrender," where they simply accept AI-generated answers without engaging in the thinking process.

Vivienne Ming, chief scientist at the Possibility Institute, raised a similar point to Business Insider in March, saying her research found most AI users rely on the technology to think less, while a minority use it to think better.

Instead, she said users should use it as a collaborator, exploring ideas, challenging assumptions, and pushing the problem forward, in what she described as "productive friction" — the process by which learning and skills form.

Nosta described a similar approach he called "iterative intelligence."

"The ability to engage with technology, with large language models, is an extraordinary opportunity for humanity to advance itself," he said.

But for that to happen, he said, people need to resist what he called the "myth" that AI's greatest value is speed and instead use it as a thinking partner, even if that means spending more time wrestling with ideas.

“大逆转”：为什么一位创新理论家说技术不再适应我们——我们正在适应它

作者：Thibault Spirlet 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

人类长期以来一直在开发技术来改变周围的世界——更快的汽车、更好的工具和更高效的机器。

人工智能可能是最早被广泛采用的技术之一，它不仅塑造了我们周围的世界，而且越来越多地影响我们思考、学习和解决问题的方式。

这是创新理论家、智库 NostaLab 创始人约翰·诺斯塔 (John Nosta) 的说法，他将这种转变称为“大逆转”。

“进步似乎越来越多地涉及让人类更好地适应我们所创造的技术世界，”诺斯塔告诉《商业内幕》。

“有机体就是项目”

他说，从历史上看，许多创新帮助人们克服了身体限制。 例如，人类发明了轮子，以便更轻松地移动重物，而汽车则极大地扩展了人们行驶的距离和速度。

诺斯塔表示，人工智能与众不同，因为它的主要影响通常是认知方面的，而不是身体方面的。 他说，人工智能不仅改变了人们的环境，而且越来越多地改变了人们思考、推理和决策的方式。

“我们现在进入了认知时代，正在改变的是思想的本质，”他说。 “从 A 到 B 的路径越来越短，我们正在将认知推迟到机器。”

他的观点与越来越多的研究相呼应，这些研究表明人工智能可以影响人们学习、记忆信息和做出决策的方式。

牛津大学出版社的研究人员去年警告说，生成式人工智能可以让学生更快、更流利，同时悄悄降低因暂停、提问和独立解决问题而产生的学习深度。

与此同时，Work AI Institute 的一份报告发现，人工智能常常会产生一种专业知识的错觉，让用户感觉自己更有能力，即使一些潜在技能开始受到侵蚀。

对于 Nosta 来说，人工智能是更广泛趋势的一个例子。 他提到了 Ozempic 等 GLP-1 药物，这些药物最初是为了治疗糖尿病而开发的，但现在广泛用于减肥，并且正在研究它们减少对酒精、尼古丁的渴望和强迫行为的潜力。

他说，一些新的创新不是重新设计环境以更好地适应人们，而是改变人类行为以帮助人们在现有环境中发挥作用。 “有机体就是项目。”

他说，这种转变对人类认知具有重要影响。

使用人工智能作为合作伙伴，而不是替代品

尽管如此，诺斯塔并不认为人工智能本质上是有害的。

他区分了所谓的“迭代智能”和“认知投降”，即人们使用人工智能通过对话来加深理解，即人们只是接受人工智能生成的答案，而不参与思考过程。

Possibility Institute 首席科学家 Vivienne Ming 在 3 月份向 Business Insider 提出了类似的观点，称她的研究发现大多数人工智能用户依靠该技术来减少思考，而少数人则利用该技术来更好地思考。

相反，她说用户应该将其用作协作者，探索想法，挑战假设，并推动问题向前发展，这就是她所描述的“富有成效的摩擦”——学习和技能形成的过程。

诺斯塔描述了一种类似的方法，他称之为“迭代智能”。

他说：“利用大型语言模型利用技术的能力，是人类自我进步的绝佳机会。”

但他说，要实现这一点，人们需要抵制他所说的人工智能最大价值是速度的“神话”，而是将其用作思考伙伴，即使这意味着要花更多时间思考想法。
